one_liner: CDF-model-based sort for numeric arrays, ~4x faster than std::sort on random data, ~15-20x on sorted/duplicate data.
what_it_does: Sorts a random-access range of numeric keys (double, int, long) in ascending order, with the same two/three-argument iterator signature as std::sort but in the learned_sort namespace. It trains a lightweight model of the data's CDF and uses it to predict each key's final bucket instead of relying purely on comparisons. It automatically falls back to std::sort for small inputs, already-sorted/reverse-sorted inputs, or when the model fails to train.
how_it_is_fast: Builds a two-layer 'recursive model index' (RMI): a root linear model plus, by default, 1000 leaf linear models trained on a 1% sample of the keys, which together approximate the empirical CDF. Each key's model-predicted CDF value picks one of ~1000 buckets directly (O(1) per key instead of O(log n) comparisons), the array is partitioned into those buckets in one pass, and each bucket is finished with std::sort/insertion sort. Separately, sort() first does a linear is_sorted/is_reverse_sorted check and returns immediately if it hits, which is why Sorted/ReverseSorted/Identical inputs are ~15-20x faster than std::sort -- that path bypasses the CDF model entirely.
when_to_use: Large batches (tens of millions+) of primitive numeric keys (double/int/long) with no attached payload
Data from a reasonably smooth/well-behaved distribution (uniform, exponential, Gaussian mixture, Zipfian, moderate duplicates) where the RMI's CDF approximation is accurate
One-off or batch/offline sorts where the model-training cost amortizes over a large input, not per-call microsorts
You can vendor a small header-only GPL-3.0 dependency and your project tolerates copyleft
x86-64 Linux/GCC builds with AVX and -march=native, matching the environment this was actually benchmarked on
when_not_to_use: Sorting records/structs with payloads or string keys -- explicitly unsupported per the README's Limitations section
Small inputs -- below roughly fanout x threshold (1000 x 100 = 100,000 elements by default) it just calls std::sort, so there's no upside
GPL-3.0 is unacceptable for the target codebase -- heavier copyleft than most sibling sort libraries in this catalog
Need active maintenance -- no commits since August 2021, all filed issues closed, unmaintained academic prototype
Sorted, reverse-sorted, or all-duplicate inputs where you want a general-purpose winner -- the project's own chart shows IS4o matching or beating LearnedSort there

integration.dependencies: none for the sort itself (STL only, include/learned_sort.h + rmi.h + utils.h); the repo's benchmark/test harness additionally pulls in Google Benchmark, Google Test, and several third-party sort implementations, but those aren't needed to call learned_sort::sort
integration.min_toolchain: C++20 (CMakeLists.txt sets CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 20); benchmarked with GCC 9.3.0-10ubuntu2
integration.platforms: Only tested on Linux (RHEL 7, Ubuntu 20.04); Release flags include -march=native -mavx, so x86-64 with AVX is assumed. A Windows/MinGW-w64 GCC10 user hit a correctness bug (issue #16), since fixed
integration.thread_safety: not documented; sort() is single-threaded with no synchronization primitives in the header, and no stated guarantee for concurrent calls on different ranges
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial -- explain: learned_sort::sort(begin, end) mirrors std::sort's iterator-pair signature exactly, but it lives in its own namespace, so every call site must change from std::sort to learned_sort::sort rather than being a transparent alias

gotchas: Automatically short-circuits to std::sort for inputs at or below ~fanout*threshold elements (100,000 by default) or when RMI training fails, so the learned path silently never runs on small inputs
The huge Sorted/ReverseSorted speedups come from an explicit is_sorted()/is_reverse_sorted() linear-scan pre-check with early return, not from the CDF model doing work

Historically had several correctness bugs specific to integer key types (slope underflow, int-division in RMI training, failures with many repeated keys) -- all filed as issues and fixed via PRs by mid-2021, but there's been no activity since to catch anything similar
No payload/tuple or string-key support (README 'Limitations'); only bare numeric arrays are sortable
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick LearnedSort over IPS4o/BlockQuicksort/x86-simd-sort/radix_sort when you have large batches (10M+) of doubles or ints from a smooth distribution and accept GPL-3.0 plus an unmaintained codebase for the ~4x win; for sorted/duplicate-heavy or adversarial data, or if you need ongoing support, IS4o matches or beats it on those inputs per LearnedSort's own benchmark chart.
verified_claims_summary: On 50M double-precision keys via Google Benchmark (GCC 9.3.0-10ubuntu2, CMake Release with -O3 -march=native -mavx, Intel Xeon Gold 6150), LearnedSort ran ~1080-1150ms vs std::sort's ~4850-5030ms (~4.2-4.6x) across Uniform, Exponential, Mixture-of-Gaussians, Zipf-0.75, and TwoDups, and ~50-60ms vs std::sort's ~750-1000ms (~15-20x) on Sorted, ReverseSorted, and Identical -- all read off the README's bar chart (plots/perf_charts.png), which prints no exact numeric labels.
status_note: Abandoned academic prototype: no commits since August 2021 and every filed issue is closed with no further activity, but it's a small header-only, GPL-3.0 library, so it's easy to vendor and freeze at the last known-good GCC 9/10 toolchain.
